The White wagtail (Motacilla alba) is a small passerine that exhibits a typical altricial developmental trajectory from a recently fertilised egg through to a free-flying fledgling. During the incubation phase, the embryonated egg is maintained at approximately 36 °C [T = 36 °C], with hatching occurring at 13 days [ab = 13 days] after the onset of incubation. This relatively brief incubation period is consistent with the fast developmental pace seen in other insectivorous birds of comparable body size. The newly emerged nestling chick weighs only 2.32 grams [Wwb = 2.32 grams], a modest body mass that demands frequent parental provisioning. This low birth weight contrasts markedly with the much greater weight at the point of first feeding, reflecting the rapid accumulation of tissue that characterises the early nestling phase. Field studies have documented that the initial wet weight immediately following hatching is 3.28 grams [Ww0 = 3.28 grams], which includes residual yolk reserves that sustain the chick during its first hours before exogenous feeding begins.

The time since birth at fledging, when the young bird achieves its first flight, is 13 days [tx = 13 days] — a relatively short nestling period that is typical for small passerines nesting in open habitats where predation risk is high at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. The downy chick undergoes rapid feather growth during this interval, transitioning from a pin-feathered nestling to a fully flight-capable fledgling. The onset of flight-feather maturation proceeds quickly, allowing the young bird to leave the nest and begin its post-fledging dispersal. This accelerated development is an ecological adaptation to the species' ground-nesting habits, where prolonged exposure on the nest would increase vulnerability to mammalian predators and corvids. The fledgling then enters a period of dependency during which it continues to be fed by parents while refining its foraging skills.

This means that birds hatched early in the breeding season are physiologically capable of reproduction within their first summer, although they rarely do so due to social constraints and the demands of territory acquisition. The post-pubertal juvenile undergoes a protracted period of behavioural maturation, learning to secure and defend a suitable nesting territory along the banks of rivers, streams, and lakeshores. The gonadal swelling associated with this transition is accompanied by a surge in circulating testosterone levels in males, which drives the development of the species' characteristic aggressive territorial displays. First-year birds that do not breed nonetheless undergo the same gonadal maturation process, ensuring that they are reproductively viable by the start of the following breeding season.

The reproductive output of the White wagtail is modest but consistent across its broad Palearctic range. Females typically lay 5 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 5 eggs per clutch], with the clutch size showing little geographic variation from western Europe through central Asia. The species usually produces 1 clutch per year [F_R_i = 1 clutch per year], although second broods are occasionally attempted when conditions are particularly favourable. This reproductive strategy — moderate clutch size combined with a single annual attempt — is characteristic of many motacillid species that invest heavily in parental care. Eggs are incubated exclusively by the female, while both parents share provisioning duties during the nestling phase. Nest success is highly variable and depends on local predation pressure and weather conditions during the vulnerable incubation and early nestling stages.

This species undertakes a significant annual migration between its breeding grounds across Eurasia and its wintering areas in sub-Saharan Africa and southern Asia, a journey that imposes substantial energetic costs. The ultimate wet weight attained by healthy adult individuals is 27.2 grams [Wwi = 27.2 grams], placing the species among the smaller members of the family Motacillidae. Adults maintain this body mass through a diet composed almost entirely of aquatic and terrestrial invertebrates, particularly Diptera larvae and small beetles, which they capture through characteristic tail-wagging foraging runs along shorelines.
